--- title: "Missing Data" subtitle: "(adapted from slides by Jason Geller and Richard McElreath)" author: "Suyog Chandramouli" categories: [Missing Data] date: '2026-04-20' institute: 'PSY504, Advanced Statistics in Psychology
Princeton University' footer: "PSY 504: Advanced Statistics" format: revealjs: theme: solarized css: slide-style.css transition: fade multiplex: false slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true fontsize: "25pt" webr: packages: ["tidyverse", "easystats", "broom", "knitr", "mice", "naniar", "ggmice", "finalfit", "marginaleffects", "skimr"] filters: - webr execute: freeze: auto echo: true message: false warning: false fig-align: center fig-width: 12 fig-height: 8 editor_options: chunk_output_type: inline code-overflow: wrap html: code-fold: true code-tools: true bibliography: references.bib editor: markdown: wrap: sentence --- ## Overview By the end of this lecture, you should be able to: - Classify missing data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, NMAR) - Diagnose missingness in your own datasets - Apply appropriate methods depending on the mechanism - Report your missing data strategy clearly ## Today ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - MCAR, MAR, NMAR - Screening data for missingness - Diagnosing missing data mechanisms in R - Missing data methods in R - Listwise deletion - Casewise deletion - Nonconditional and conditional imputation - Multiple imputation - Maximum likelihood - Reporting ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![Richard McElreath](images/terminator.png){fig-align="center" width="296"} ::: ::::: ## Discuss Have you ever had to deal with missing data in your studies or in your dataset? - What caused it? - How did you deal with it? ::: {.notes} The way missing data arise determines which statistical tools give valid results and which ones mislead you. Get students talking before the formal framework. ::: ## Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("mice") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(easystats) library(knitr) library(broom) library(ggmice) library(mice) library(naniar) library(finalfit) ``` ::: - QMD available in: ::: {.notes} - `mice` = Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (workhorse for imputation) - `naniar` = purpose-built for exploring/visualizing missing data (`vis_miss()`, `mcar_test()`, `gg_miss_var()`) - `ggmice` = visualization companion to `mice` -- plots imputed vs. observed values, convergence diagnostics, density comparisons across imputed datasets - `finalfit` = clinical research package whose `missing_pairs()` and `missing_pattern()` functions diagnose missingness mechanisms by comparing distributions split by whether a variable is missing - All three are built specifically for missing data workflows, not general tools repurposed ::: # Missing Data Mechanisms {.center} ## Rubin's Framework ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Rubin proposed we can divide any data set $Y$ into two components: - $Y_\text{obs}$ the observed values - $Y_\text{mis}$ the missing values $$Y = Y_\text{obs} + Y_\text{mis}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%207.46.41%20AM.png){fig-align="center"} Every analysis implicitly assumes something about $Y_\text{mis}$. This decomposition forces that assumption into the open. ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Why data are missing matters as much as how much is missing. The mechanism you're dealing with determines which methods produce valid results. The decomposition turns an invisible assumption into an explicit modeling choice. ::: ## Missing data mechanisms - Mechanisms describe how missingness relates to the data - ***Mechanisms function as statistical assumptions*** - This framework is the theoretical backbone for accounting for missing data ::: {.notes} The mechanism is not something you test for definitively; it is an assumption you argue for based on your knowledge of the data-generating process. ::: ## Dog & Homework example (3 mechanisms) ![](images/DogHomework_DAG.png){fig-align="center"} The critical question: **what determines whether data goes missing?** ::: {.notes} McElreath's metaphor: **a dog eats homework**. The three mechanisms differ in **what drives the dog's eating behavior**. The DAG shows the causal structure behind each one. ::: ## Missing completely at random (MCAR) ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - **Dog eats homework randomly** - No relationship between missingness and any values - Loss of precision, but usually no bias - Complete-case analysis (**= listwise deletion**) is valid ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_09.jpeg){fig-align="center"} The cause may be known (e.g., coffee spilled on questionnaires) -- what matters is that the cause is unrelated to any variable in the data. ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Under MCAR, complete cases are a random subsample of the full data, so any statistic you compute is unbiased. You lose power (fewer observations, larger SEs) but not accuracy. MCAR doesn't mean the cause is unknown -- it means the cause has nothing to do with the data values. ::: ## MCAR visualized ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/mcar.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_11.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Left: DAG with no arrows into the missingness indicator. Right: McElreath's simulation showing posteriors centered on the true values even after dropping incomplete cases. - MCAR is the "best case" in the sense of being most forgiving -- hard to get wrong, any method works - But NOT best for estimation quality: MAR data handled with MI/ML can produce better estimates than MCAR data handled with listwise deletion, because MI/ML uses all observed information (including partial records) while deletion throws them away - "Best case" = most robust to naive methods, not best possible estimates ::: ## ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_12.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} Wider posteriors (less precision) but still centered on the truth. MCAR means the observed data are a random subsample of the full data. ::: ## Conditionally missing at random (CMAR) ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - Missingness depends on observed data - **Dog eats conditional on cause of homework** - Valid inference if we condition correctly - **The name "Missing at Random" is misleading**: missingness is not random unconditionally, only **after** conditioning on observed variables ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_14.jpeg){fig-align="center"} ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} MAR means missingness depends on other observed variables but not on the missing values themselves. **The dog eats homework based on something you can measure.** Once you account for that variable, the remaining missingness is random. ::: ## CMAR: Simulation evidence ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_16.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} Under MAR, simply dropping incomplete cases biases estimates. The complete cases are a non-random subsample. ::: ## ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_17.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} But if we properly condition on the variables that predict missingness, we recover unbiased results. The fix requires modeling the relationship between missingness and observed data. ::: ## CMAR visualized ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/cmar.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} - Sometimes the missingness-predictor relationship is nonlinear - Poor modeling of MAR can still lead to bias - MI and ML handle this because they model the joint distribution ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} DAG shows an arrow from an observed variable into the missingness indicator. Because we can measure what drives missingness, we can adjust for it. But the adjustment must be flexible enough to capture the true relationship. ::: ## Not missing at random (NMAR) ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - Missingness depends on the missing values *themselves* - **Dog eats conditional on homework itself** - Produces bias in standard analyses - The missingness pattern is **informative**: who is missing tells you something about the values that are missing ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_19.jpeg){fig-align="center"} ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} A depressed person doesn't fill out the depression questionnaire because they're depressed. No observed variable can explain it away. Standard methods fail because they can't access the information locked in the missing values. ::: ## NMAR visualized ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/nmar.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/Mcelreath/Lecture_18_Page_21.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Left: DAG with arrow from the missing value itself into the missingness indicator. Right: simulation showing both naive deletion and standard adjustments give biased results under NMAR. ::: # Workflow for Missing Data {.center} ## Three steps 1. **Identify** missing data (and how much) 2. **Diagnose** the mechanism (MCAR? MAR? NMAR?) 3. **Account for** missingness: - Deletion (not recommended) - Imputation - Maximum likelihood - Bayesian methods (model observed + missing jointly) # Data {.center} ## Chronic pain example - Enders (2023): *N* = 275, psychological correlates of chronic pain - Depression (`depress`) and perceived control (`control`) - Perceived control is complete; depression scores are missing ::: callout-note Dataset manipulated so missingness is related to control (low control = missing depression). MAR by construction. ::: ## Loading the data ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- read.table("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jgeller112/PSY504-Advanced-Stats-S24/main/slides/03-Missing_Data/APA%20Missing%20Data%20Training/Analysis%20Examples/pain.dat", na.strings = "999") names(dat) <- c("id", "txgrp", "male", "age", "edugroup", "workhrs", "exercise", "paingrps", "pain", "anxiety", "stress", "control", "depress", "interfere", "disability", paste0("dep", seq(1:7)), paste0("int", seq(1:6)), paste0("dis", seq(1:6))) dat <- dat %>% select("id", "age", "control", "depress", "stress") %>% mutate(depress=ifelse(depress==999, NA, depress)) %>% mutate(r_mar_low = ifelse(control < 15.51, 1, 0)) %>% mutate(depress = ifelse(r_mar_low == 1, NA, depress)) %>% select(-r_mar_low) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | id| age| control| depress| stress| |--:|---:|-------:|-------:|------:| | 1| 68| 13| NA| 5| | 2| 38| 19| 28| 7| | 3| 31| 20| 8| 4| | 4| 31| 17| 28| 7| | 5| 58| 22| 12| 3| | 6| 63| 26| 13| 5| | 7| 38| 16| 23| 5| | 8| 54| 30| 12| 1| | 9| 66| 20| 9| 3| | 10| 31| 27| NA| 2| ::: ::: ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Walking through the code: - `read.table(...)`: loads the raw pain dataset from Enders (2023); `na.strings = "999"` tells R that 999 is the missing data code in the original file - `names(dat) <- c(...)`: the raw file has no column headers, so we assign meaningful variable names (id, treatment group, demographics, pain measures, depression items, etc.) - `paste0("dep", seq(1:7))`: creates names `dep1` through `dep7` for individual depression items (same pattern for interference and disability items) - `select(...)`: keeps only the five variables we need: id, age, control, depression, stress - `mutate(depress = ifelse(depress==999, NA, depress))`: converts any remaining 999 codes to proper `NA` values - `mutate(r_mar_low = ifelse(control < 15.51, 1, 0))`: creates a flag for low perceived control - `mutate(depress = ifelse(r_mar_low == 1, NA, depress))`: **this is where we artificially introduce MAR** -- anyone with control below 15.51 gets their depression score set to missing - `select(-r_mar_low)`: drops the helper flag so it doesn't appear in the analysis data The result: a clean dataset where missingness on depression is driven by perceived control (MAR by construction). ::: ## EDA - What variables have missing data? How much? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(naniar) vis_miss(dat) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Missing_Data_2026_Lecture_Narrated_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `vis_miss(dat)`: from `naniar`, creates a heatmap where each row is an observation and each column is a variable - Dark cells = missing values; light cells = observed - Gives an immediate visual summary: `depress` has substantial missingness, other variables are complete - The percentage at the top tells you overall missingness rate ::: ## EDA: Summary statistics ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(skimr) skimr::skim(dat) %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |skim_type |skim_variable | n_missing| complete_rate| numeric.mean| numeric.sd| numeric.p0| numeric.p25| numeric.p50| numeric.p75| numeric.p100|numeric.hist | |:---------|:-------------|---------:|-------------:|------------:|----------:|----------:|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|------------:|:------------| |numeric |id | 0| 1.00| 138.000000| 79.529869| 1| 69.5| 138| 206.5| 275|▇▇▇▇▇ | |numeric |age | 0| 1.00| 45.643636| 11.271221| 19| 38.0| 46| 53.0| 78|▂▇▇▃▁ | |numeric |control | 0| 1.00| 20.763636| 5.252610| 6| 17.0| 21| 25.0| 30|▁▃▇▇▅ | |numeric |depress | 77| 0.72| 14.303030| 6.058018| 7| 9.0| 13| 18.0| 28|▇▆▂▂▂ | |numeric |stress | 0| 1.00| 3.901818| 1.802623| 1| 3.0| 4| 5.0| 7|▇▅▇▅▆ | ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `skim()`: from `skimr`, produces a summary table with n_missing, complete_rate, mean, sd, and percentiles for each variable - Complements `vis_miss()` -- the heatmap shows the pattern, `skim()` gives you the numbers ::: ## Missing patterns ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - Pattern matrix: structure of observed and missing values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat %>% plot_pattern() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Missing_Data_2026_Lecture_Narrated_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/missing_patterns.png){fig-align='center' width=495} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} - `plot_pattern()`: from `ggmice`, shows which combinations of variables are observed (1) vs. missing (0) - Each row in the plot is a unique missingness pattern; the number on the left is how many cases have that pattern - Our data has a simple univariate pattern: only `depress` is incomplete ::: ## Types of missing patterns ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - **Univariate**: one variable with missing data - **Monotone**: if variable *j* is missing, all subsequent are too - Common in longitudinal dropout - **Non-monotone**: scattered, no systematic ordering ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/new_patterns.webp){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Is it MCAR or MAR? ![](images/marcar.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} Flowchart for diagnostic logic. Test for MCAR; if rejected, investigate whether MAR is plausible by examining relationships between missingness and observed variables. ::: ## Little's MCAR test - Little's test: $\chi^2$ statistic - Significant = not MCAR - Not significant = consistent with MCAR ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(naniar) mcar_test(dat) %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | statistic| df| p.value| missing.patterns| |---------:|--:|-------:|----------------:| | 66.38158| 4| 0| 2| ::: ::: - Not used much anymore! ::: {.notes} - `mcar_test(dat)`: from `naniar`, runs Little's MCAR test - Returns a chi-square statistic, df, and p-value - Significant p = reject MCAR; non-significant = consistent with MCAR (but doesn't confirm it) - Limitations: low power, tests all variables at once, non-significance is not evidence for MCAR ::: ## Visual diagnostics ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(finalfit) explanatory = c("control", "age") dependent = "depress" misspairs <- dat %>% missing_pairs(explanatory, dependent) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Missing_Data_2026_Lecture_Narrated_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `missing_pairs(explanatory, dependent)`: from `finalfit`, creates paired density/box plots - Each panel compares the distribution of an explanatory variable (control, age) split by whether `depress` is missing (blue) or observed (red) - If the two distributions differ visually, missingness is related to that variable -- evidence for MAR ::: ## Dummy variable approach - Create binary indicator: 1 = missing, 0 = observed - If related to other variables, evidence for MAR ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pain_r <- dat %>% mutate(depress_1 = ifelse(is.na(depress), 1, 0)) pain_r %>% head() %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | id| age| control| depress| stress| depress_1| |--:|---:|-------:|-------:|------:|---------:| | 1| 68| 13| NA| 5| 1| | 2| 38| 19| 28| 7| 0| | 3| 31| 20| 8| 4| 0| | 4| 31| 17| 28| 7| 0| | 5| 58| 22| 12| 3| 0| | 6| 63| 26| 13| 5| 0| ::: ::: ## Testing ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model <- lm(control~depress_1, data=pain_r) tidy(model) %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|---------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 22.348485| 0.3270999| 68.323107| 0| |depress_1 | -5.660173| 0.6181608| -9.156474| 0| ::: ::: - Missing on depression is related to control! ::: {.notes} - `mutate(depress_1 = ifelse(is.na(depress), 1, 0))`: creates a binary indicator -- 1 if depression is missing, 0 if observed - `lm(control ~ depress_1)`: regresses perceived control on the missingness indicator - Significant coefficient means control differs between the missing and observed groups -- evidence for MAR - You could also use a t-test or logistic regression here; the logic is the same ::: # Methods for MCAR {.center} ## Listwise deletion ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat %>% head(10) %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | id| age| control| depress| stress| |--:|---:|-------:|-------:|------:| | 1| 68| 13| NA| 5| | 2| 38| 19| 28| 7| | 3| 31| 20| 8| 4| | 4| 31| 17| 28| 7| | 5| 58| 22| 12| 3| | 6| 63| 26| 13| 5| | 7| 38| 16| 23| 5| | 8| 54| 30| 12| 1| | 9| 66| 20| 9| 3| | 10| 31| 27| NA| 2| ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat %>% drop_na() %>% head(10) %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | id| age| control| depress| stress| |--:|---:|-------:|-------:|------:| | 2| 38| 19| 28| 7| | 3| 31| 20| 8| 4| | 4| 31| 17| 28| 7| | 5| 58| 22| 12| 3| | 6| 63| 26| 13| 5| | 7| 38| 16| 23| 5| | 8| 54| 30| 12| 1| | 9| 66| 20| 9| 3| | 11| 37| 25| 21| 7| | 13| 33| 17| 20| 4| ::: ::: ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Removes any row with a missing value. Under MCAR, remaining cases are a random subsample so estimates are unbiased. Under MAR/NMAR, the subsample is non-random and estimates are biased. ::: ## Listwise deletion: pros and cons - Pros: unbiased if MCAR - Cons: can lose substantial data; biased if not MCAR ## Casewise (pairwise) deletion - Delete only observations where the missing data is relevant to *that specific comparison* - Pros: preserves more data; unbiased under MCAR - Cons: each statistic uses a different subset; can produce non-positive-definite covariance matrices ::: {.notes} Each entry in a correlation matrix uses all cases with both variables observed. Results may be internally inconsistent. ::: # Methods for MAR {.center} ## Unconditional (mean) imputation -- Bad - Replace missing values with the mean of observed values ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- c(5, 8, 3, NA, NA) d_mean <- mean(d, na.rm = TRUE) d_mean_imp <- ifelse(is.na(d), d_mean, d) d_mean_imp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.000000 8.000000 3.000000 5.333333 5.333333 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sd(d, na.rm=TRUE) # sd of original ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.516611 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sd(d_mean_imp) # sd after mean imputation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.779513 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Shrinks variance, makes SEs too small, inflates Type I error. Distorts relationships between variables. Almost never appropriate. ::: ## Conditional imputation (regression) ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - Use observed variables to predict missing values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lm(depress~control) imp.regress <- mice(dat, method="norm.predict", m=1, maxit=1) ``` ::: - Missing scores receive predicted values ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/reg_imp.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Like interpolation: fills in values using the trend. Problem: all imputed values fall on the regression line with no residual scatter, underestimating variability. ::: ## Stochastic Regression - Adds a random residual to predicted values - More realistic standard errors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mice(data, m=1, method="norm.nob") ``` ::: ![](images/stoch_reg.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} Better than deterministic regression, but a single imputation still treats imputed values as if they were real data. We need multiple imputations to capture imputation uncertainty. ::: # Multiple Imputation {.center} ## The idea - Use multiple plausible values instead of one "best guess" - Creates *m* completed datasets, each with different imputed values - Captures uncertainty about what the missing values might have been ## Step 1: Impute Create *m* imputed datasets with `mice()` ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.05.58%20PM.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} Each dataset gets different plausible imputed values, drawn from a predictive distribution fitted to the observed data. ::: ## Step 2: Analyze Fit your model to each dataset with `with()` ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.06.45%20PM.png){fig-align="center"} ## Step 3: Pool Combine results with `pool()` using Rubin's rules ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.07.17%20PM.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} Rubin's rules combine within-imputation variance (usual sampling variability) and between-imputation variance (extra uncertainty from missing data). ::: ## Multiple Imputation summary ![](images/mice_comp.PNG){fig-align="center" width="666"} ## Connection to the Bootstrap - Both generate multiple datasets, analyze each separately, pool results - Bootstrap: "what if we'd drawn a different sample?" - MI: "what if the missing values had been different?" ::: {.notes} Can be combined into bootstrap multiple imputation. ::: ## 1. Impute with `mice` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m = 5 imp <- mice(dat, m = m, seed = 24415, method="pmm", print = FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str(imp, max.level = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` List of 23 $ data :'data.frame': 275 obs. of 5 variables: $ imp :List of 5 $ m : num 5 $ where : logi [1:275, 1:5] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ... ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2 $ blocks :List of 5 $ call : language mice(data = dat, m = m, method = "pmm", printFlag = FALSE, seed = 24415) $ nmis : Named int [1:5] 0 0 0 77 0 ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:5] "id" "age" "control" "depress" ... $ method : Named chr [1:5] "" "" "" "pmm" ... ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:5] "id" "age" "control" "depress" ... $ predictorMatrix: num [1:5, 1:5] 0 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 1 ... ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2 $ visitSequence : chr [1:5] "id" "age" "control" "depress" ... $ formulas :List of 5 $ calltype : Named chr [1:5] "pred" "pred" "pred" "pred" ... ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:5] "id" "age" "control" "depress" ... $ post : Named chr [1:5] "" "" "" "" ... ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:5] "id" "age" "control" "depress" ... $ blots :List of 5 $ ignore : logi [1:275] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ... $ seed : num 24415 $ iteration : num 5 $ lastSeedValue : int [1:626] 10403 359 1009391010 -1973990381 908174720 -738124646 251387381 -1899514340 395796544 1088258267 ... $ chainMean : num [1:5, 1:5, 1:5] NaN NaN NaN 16.8 NaN ... ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 3 $ chainVar : num [1:5, 1:5, 1:5] NA NA NA 47.1 NA ... ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 3 $ loggedEvents : NULL $ version :Classes 'package_version', 'numeric_version' hidden list of 1 $ date : Date[1:1], format: "2026-04-20" - attr(*, "class")= chr "mids" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `mice(dat, m = 5, ...)`: creates 5 multiply imputed datasets - `seed = 24415`: makes results reproducible - `method = "pmm"`: predictive mean matching (default, works well for continuous data) - `print = FALSE`: suppresses iteration output - `str(imp, max.level = 1)`: shows the structure -- `imp` is a `mids` object containing imputed values, the original data, and metadata about the imputation process ::: ## 1. Impute with `mice` (cont.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str(imp$imp, max.level = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` List of 5 $ id :'data.frame': 0 obs. of 5 variables: $ age :'data.frame': 0 obs. of 5 variables: $ control:'data.frame': 0 obs. of 5 variables: $ depress:'data.frame': 77 obs. of 5 variables: $ stress :'data.frame': 0 obs. of 5 variables: ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(imp$imp$depress) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 4 5 1 28 26 18 21 13 10 12 7 8 14 8 12 19 23 10 11 27 14 24 27 20 21 27 15 19 14 15 14 12 24 26 13 8 13 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `imp$imp`: a list of data frames, one per variable that was imputed - `imp$imp$depress`: the imputed depression values; each column is one of the 5 datasets, each row is a case that had missing data - Values differ across columns because each imputation is a separate stochastic draw - `complete(imp, "all")` (commented out) would extract all 5 full datasets as a list ::: ## PMM ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - Predictive mean matching - Fit regression on observed data - Predict mean for the missing case - Find "donor" cases with closest predicted means - Use a donor's actual observed value ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/PMM.PNG){width="435" height="319"} ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} PMM always produces plausible values (they're real observed values from donors) and handles non-normal distributions well. ::: ## 2. Model with `mice` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- with(data = imp, expr = lm(depress ~ control)) summary(fit) %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| nobs| df.residual| |:-----------|----------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|----:|-----------:| |(Intercept) | 26.5853480| 1.3951117| 19.056071| 0| 275| 273| |control | -0.5579633| 0.0651453| -8.564900| 0| 275| 273| |(Intercept) | 26.3445428| 1.4404262| 18.289409| 0| 275| 273| |control | -0.5397109| 0.0672613| -8.024091| 0| 275| 273| |(Intercept) | 24.9087161| 1.4261998| 17.465096| 0| 275| 273| |control | -0.4880730| 0.0665970| -7.328753| 0| 275| 273| |(Intercept) | 24.3346289| 1.3947519| 17.447282| 0| 275| 273| |control | -0.4644524| 0.0651285| -7.131319| 0| 275| 273| |(Intercept) | 24.9290442| 1.3967357| 17.848076| 0| 275| 273| |control | -0.4862499| 0.0652212| -7.455400| 0| 275| 273| ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `with(data = imp, expr = lm(depress ~ control))`: fits `lm(depress ~ control)` separately to each of the 5 imputed datasets - Returns a list of 5 model fits - `summary(fit)` shows the coefficients from each fit side by side ::: ## 3. `mice` Pool Results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result <- pool(fit) model_parameters(result) %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Parameter | Coefficient| SE| CI| CI_low| CI_high| t| df_error| p| |:-----------|-----------:|---------:|----:|----------:|---------:|--------:|--------:|-----:| |(Intercept) | 25.4204560| 1.7771524| 0.95| 21.7601261| 29.080786| 14.30404| 24.97094| 0e+00| |control | -0.5072899| 0.0788639| 0.95| -0.6673029| -0.347277| -6.43247| 35.55542| 2e-07| ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `pool(fit)`: combines the 5 sets of estimates using Rubin's rules - `model_parameters(result)`: from `easystats`, gives a clean summary table with pooled coefficients, SEs, CIs, and p-values - The pooled SE is larger than any individual SE because it includes between-imputation variance (the extra uncertainty from not knowing the true missing values) ::: ## 3. `mice` Pool Results (cont.) - `emmeans` does not work with `mice` objects - Use `marginaleffects` instead ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(marginaleffects) mfx_mice <- avg_slopes(fit) mfx_mice %>% kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term |contrast | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| s.value| df| conf.low| conf.high| |:-------|:--------|----------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|--------:|--------:|----------:|----------:| |control |dY/dX | -0.5072899| 0.0788632| -6.432533| 2e-07| 22.29173| 35.55424| -0.6673015| -0.3472783| ::: ::: ## Plot Imputations - Make sure imputed values look similar to real data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggmice(imp, ggplot2::aes(x = .imp, y = depress)) + ggplot2::geom_jitter() + labs(x = "Imputation number") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Missing_Data_2026_Lecture_Narrated_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `ggmice(imp, aes(x = .imp, y = depress))`: plots depression values grouped by imputation number - `.imp = 0` is the original (observed) data; `.imp = 1-5` are the imputed datasets - Blue dots = imputed values; red dots = observed values - Imputed values should have a similar range, center, and spread as observed - If imputed values cluster in a narrow range or extend well beyond the observed range, the imputation model may be misspecified ::: # Maximum Likelihood (ML) {.center} ## ML - Finds most probable parameter estimates given the observed data - Each observation contributes whatever data it has - No imputation performed ::: {.notes} ML is a principled approach that uses all available information. It sidesteps imputation entirely by working with the incomplete data directly. ::: ## How ML uses partial data No values are filled in. The correlation structure implies what missing values probably look like, without writing a number into any empty cell. ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.30.44%20PM.png){fig-align="center" width="538"} ::: {.notes} The likelihood function integrates over possible values of the missing data, weighted by their plausibility given observed data and the assumed distribution (usually multivariate normal). ::: ## Chronic pain illustration - Low perceived control = more likely to have missing depression (MAR) - True means are both 20 ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.31.57%20PM.png){fig-align="center" width="598"} ## Deleting incomplete information ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - Deletion gives a non-representative sample - Control mean too high (23.1), depression mean too low (17.2) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.34.18%20PM.png){fig-align="center" width="607"} ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Selectively removing participants with low control over-represents the high-control group, biasing both means. ::: ## Partial data - Partial data records primarily have low perceived control scores ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.35.03%20PM.png){fig-align="center" width="605"} ::: {.notes} Even without depression scores, these participants' control scores carry information about the joint distribution. ::: ## Adjusting perceived control - Low control scores increase variability, pull the mean downward ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.36.26%20PM.png){fig-align="center"} ## How ML infers missing values - Multivariate normality + negative correlation: low control implies high depression ![](images/Screen%20Shot%202024-01-04%20at%205.37.37%20PM.png){fig-align="center"} ::: {.notes} Observed control scores "pull" the depression distribution toward what the missing values should look like, given the correlation structure. ::: ## Adjusting Depression Distribution - Depression mean and variance increase to accommodate the implied high scores ![](images/ML_unbiased.png){fig-align="center" width="559"} ::: {.notes} Unbiased parameter estimates, recovered from incomplete data without ever imputing a single value. ::: ## ML: Cons - Limited to normal data; mixed metric options are less common - Biased with interactions and non-linear terms - MLM software often discards observations with missing predictors ::: {.notes} ML is a good default for simple models with continuous normal outcomes, but MI may be more flexible for complex models. ::: ## A note on hierarchical models - HLMs handle unbalanced designs gracefully (ragged longitudinal data) - Often confused with handling missing data, but HLMs still assume MAR - If dropout depends on the outcome (NMAR), HLMs are biased too ## Distinguish between NMAR and MAR - It's genuinely difficult - Not many good techniques - Strategies to convert NMAR to MAR: - Track down the missing data - Find auxiliary variables - Collect more data explaining missingness ::: {.notes} NMAR involves information we cannot observe. Sensitivity analysis (fitting models under both MAR and NMAR assumptions) is often the best we can do. ::: ## Distinguish between NMAR and MAR ![](images/reddit.jpg){fig-align="center"} ## Bayesian Methods ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Without Missing Data** - y_i ~ Normal(α + βx_i, σ²) - α ~ Normal(0, 10) - β ~ Normal(0, 1) - σ ~ HalfCauchy(0, 5) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **With Missing Data** - y_i ~ Normal(α + βx_i, σ²) - x_i ~ Normal(μx, τ²) for missing x_i - α ~ Normal(0, 10) - β ~ Normal(0, 1) - σ ~ HalfCauchy(0, 5) - μx ~ Normal(0, 10) - τ ~ HalfCauchy(0, 5) ::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Missing values are treated as parameters. MCMC sampling gives posteriors for all parameters, automatically integrating over uncertainty about what the missing values might have been. ::: ## Reporting Missing Data - Template from [Stef van Buuren](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-reporting.html) ::: callout-tip The *percentage of missing values* across the nine variables varied between *0 and 34%*. In total *1601 out of 3801 records (42%)* were incomplete. Many girls had no score because the nurse felt that the measurement was "unnecessary," or because the girl did not give permission. Older girls had many more missing data. We used *multiple imputation* to create and analyze *40 multiply imputed datasets*. Methodologists currently regard multiple imputation as a state-of-the-art technique because it improves accuracy and statistical power relative to other missing data techniques. *Incomplete variables were imputed under fully conditional specification, using the default settings of the mice 3.0 package (Van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011)*. The parameters of substantive interest were estimated in each imputed dataset separately, and combined using Rubin's rules. For comparison, *we also performed the analysis on the subset of complete cases.* ::: ## What to report - *Amount of missing data* (overall and per variable) - *Reasons for missingness* - *Consequences* (assumed mechanism and why) - *Method* (MI, ML, Bayesian, etc.) - *Imputation model* (variables, method) - *Pooling* (Rubin's rules, etc.) - *Software* (package versions) - *Complete-case analysis* (sensitivity check) ## Is it MCAR, MAR, NMAR? > The post-experiment manipulation-check questionnaires for five participants were accidentally thrown away. . . . - **MCAR** -- accidental, unrelated to any variable ## Is it MCAR, MAR, NMAR? > In a 2-day memory experiment, people who know they would do poorly on the memory test are discouraged and don't want to return for the second session . . . - **NMAR** -- missingness depends on the unobserved memory scores ## Is it MCAR, MAR, NMAR? > A health psychologist is surveying high school students on marijuana use. Students who scored highly on anxiety left these questions blank. . . . - **MAR** -- missingness depends on anxiety, an observed variable ## Wrap up - When you have missing data, think about **why** they are missing - Missing data handled improperly can bias your estimates - MI and ML are good ways to handle missing data! - Bayesian methods are good too :) - Inverse probability weighting seem to work well [@gomila2022] - Always report your missing data strategy transparently

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
